desc:
The lowest common ancestor (LCA) of two nodes p and q in a binary tree is the deepest node that has both of them in its subtree. A node counts as part of its own subtree, so if p is an ancestor of q then the LCA is p itself.

Given the tree and the values p and q (both occur in the tree; they may be equal), return the value of their lowest common ancestor.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right). A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For the tree below ([3, 5, 1, 6, 2, 0, 8, -1, -1, 7, 4]): p = 5, q = 1 gives 3, and p = 5, q = 4 gives 5.

        3
      /   \
     5     1
    / \   / \
   6   2 0   8
      / \
     7   4
constraints: All node values are distinct, so a value identifies exactly one node
The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
p and q occur in the tree (possibly p == q)
hints: Think of the path from the root to each of the two nodes. Where do the two paths split?
If you know the depth and the parent of every node, you can move the deeper node up until both are on the same depth.

After equalising depths, move both nodes up one parent at a time until they are the same node. That node is the LCA. With level order, parents come before children, so depth and parent arrays take a single pass to fill.
editorial: Compute parent and depth of every node. To find the LCA of a and b, lift the deeper node until the depths are equal, then lift both together until they meet. This is O(n) to prepare and O(depth) per query.

The classic recursive solution does the same without extra arrays: lca(node) returns the node if it is p or q; otherwise it asks both subtrees, and if both return something, the current node is the split point. If only one side returns something, pass that result up. Either way each node is looked at once.
